questions.q: What is the core difference between the liberal view of citizenship and the communitarian view regarding the source of individual identity?
questions.a: The liberal view sees the individual as prior to society, with identity formed independently; the communitarian view sees identity as constituted by community values and traditions. A wrong answer (e.g., "both agree identity comes from community") reveals confusion about the ontological priority of individual vs community.

questions.q: Why do civic republicans argue that citizenship requires active participation in public affairs, not just voting?
questions.a: Civic republicans believe freedom is realized through self-government; passive enjoyment of rights leads to corruption and loss of liberty. A wrong answer (e.g., "voting is enough") shows misunderstanding of civic virtue as continuous engagement.

questions.q: A state passes a law requiring all citizens to perform one year of mandatory community service. Which view—liberal, communitarian, or civic republican—would most strongly support this, and why?
questions.a: Civic republican (and communitarian) would support it as cultivating civic virtue and shared responsibility; liberal would oppose as coercive violation of individual liberty. A wrong answer indicates inability to map theoretical positions to policy.

questions.q: Compare how the Indian Constitution's Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) reflect communitarian and civic republican ideas rather than purely liberal ones.
questions.a: Article 51A imposes duties like promoting harmony, protecting environment, and developing scientific temper—emphasizing obligations to community and active citizenship, not just rights. A wrong answer misses the non-liberal character of enforceable moral duties.

questions.q: Evaluate the criticism that communitarian citizenship may justify majoritarian imposition on minorities. Use the Indian context of uniform civil code debates.
questions.a: Communitarian emphasis on shared values can marginalize minority cultures; in India, UCC debates pit national integration against minority personal laws. A balanced evaluation acknowledges both integrationist and pluralist concerns. A wrong answer shows uncritical acceptance or rejection without nuance.

questions.q: Draft a one-paragraph preamble for a hypothetical "Citizen's Charter" for a model Indian village that blends liberal rights, communitarian values, and civic republican duties.
questions.a: A good answer includes: individual rights (speech, equality), community commitments (shared festivals, mutual aid), and participatory duties (gram sabha attendance, transparency). A poor answer lists only rights or only duties, missing the synthesis.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The ______ view of citizenship emphasizes that citizenship is rooted in shared community values, traditions, and social obligations, arguing that individual identity and rights are shaped by the community.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a Resident Welfare Association (RWA) meeting in your Delhi neighbourhood debating whether to make waste ______ mandatory.

Fill in the blank: Start by asking: "When the RWA votes, are we exercising a right or fulfilling a duty?" Connect this to the liberal view (node ______) which prioritizes individual rights, then introduce how communitarians like Michael Sandel and civic republicans like Quentin Skinner re-center community and participation.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can distinguish communitarian and civic republican perspectives from the liberal view, explain how each redefines the relationship between rights and obligations, and apply these frameworks to evaluate contemporary Indian debates on citizenship (e.g., uniform civil code, fundamental duties, participatory governance).
